No slides were given for this lecture. The notes of Alessa, Alsalamah and Alomar word for word, in their own order (green), every gift (red) under the part it belongs to.

Notes

Atherosclerosis: Pathophysiology

DEFINITION
Atherosclerosis = a chronic inflammatory disease of large and medium-sized arteries → plaque formation → arterial narrowing / occlusion → reduced blood flow. Disease of small vessels is classified separately as microangiopathy.
Notes

Plaque development — the cascade

1 Endothelial injury Chemical or mechanical injury → inflammation; lipid and WBCs gather in the subendothelial space.→2 Foam cells → fatty streak Macrophages engulf lipid → foam cells → fatty streak and further inflammation.→3 Fibrous plaque Inflammatory cells, smooth muscle cells, fibroblasts and calcium are recruited.→4 Progressive stenosis Growing plaque narrows the lumen → reduced distal flow.→5 Rupture & thrombosis Exposed thrombogenic material → platelet adhesion & aggregation → thrombus → occlusion.
TREATMENT LINK
Antiplatelets act at step 5 only: they prevent platelet-mediated thrombosis. They do not prevent lipid or inflammatory-cell accumulation, so they don't treat the plaque itself.
Notes

Risk factors

Non-modifiable Increasing age Male sex Family history / genetic predisposition·Modifiable — MAJOR (memorize) Diabetes mellitus Smoking Hypertension Dyslipidemia·Modifiable — additional Obesity Physical inactivity Insulin resistance

Atherosclerotic burden varies between individuals because genetic and acquired risk factors act in combination.

  • The most important modifiable major risk factor among the options → diabetes mellitus (obesity is minor; family history and male sex aren't modifiable). 438
Notes

PAD: Significance & Prognosis

DEFINITION
PAD = atherosclerotic obstruction of the lower-limb arterial circulation, including the aorta and its distal branches.
THE BIG IDEA — PAD IS A MARKER OF SYSTEMIC ATHEROSCLEROSIS
Atherosclerosis often involves several vascular beds at once → PAD is associated with coronary artery disease, cerebrovascular disease, MI, stroke and increased mortality.
Leg disease can reveal otherwise unrecognized coronary or cerebrovascular disease.
PAD patients are at risk of both MI and stroke — MI is generally the more frequent event.
Cardiovascular events and death are more common than progression to major limb intervention or amputation.
The leg pulse examination is an accessible window onto arterial disease — unlike the coronaries, which can't be palpated.
Most PAD patients are asymptomatic → detecting them allows early, aggressive cardiovascular risk reduction.
PAD limits walking, function and quality of life; the associated systemic disease limits survival.
Greater PAD severity → higher CV morbidity and mortality, even when limb symptoms are limited.
Notes

Mortality & natural history

~25% MORTALITY AT 5 YEARS·~50% AT 10 YEARS·~75% AT 15 YEARS·6–7% ANNUAL MORTALITY

Figures as presented in the lecture.

RULE OF THUMB
Prognosis tracks disease burden and symptoms: asymptomatic PAD survives better than symptomatic PAD, and severe symptoms mean a poorer prognosis. A PAD patient is more likely to die of an MI or stroke than to lose the leg.
Notes

Clinical Presentation

The clinical spectrum, from least to most severe:

Asymptomatic The majority — despite arterial disease or reduced / absent pulses.→Intermittent claudication Reproducible exertional muscle pain, relieved by rest.→CLTI Ischemic rest pain Pain without exertion.→CLTI Ulceration / tissue loss Tissue defect with a visible base.→CLTI Gangrene Tissue necrosis.
  • Leriche syndrome — absent femoral pulses + bilateral claudication + impotence. 438 ×2
Notes

Asymptomatic PAD

DON'T BE FALSELY REASSURED
Most patients have no typical symptoms despite arterial disease or reduced / absent pulses. Limited physical activity can conceal ischemia, so the absence of claudication does not exclude significant PAD.
Notes

Intermittent claudication

DEFINITION
Intermittent claudication = reproducible, exercise-induced muscle pain caused by insufficient arterial supply and relieved by rest. It arises in the exercising muscles supplied by the diseased artery, so its location localizes the obstruction.

Claudication distance = the walking distance before pain develops. It is reproducible at a given disease severity and shrinks as atherosclerosis progresses (e.g. 1 km → 500 m → 200 m).

Pain localization — where it hurts tells you where the lesion is:

Level of arterial diseaseClaudication siteWhy
Aortoiliac / common iliacButtock / glutealLesion lies above the internal iliac origin → gluteal muscles under-perfused
External iliac / proximal femoralThigh (or more distal muscles)Internal iliac supply is intact → gluteal perfusion may be preserved
More distal diseaseCalf / legOnly the distal muscle territory is ischemic

Vascular vs neurogenic claudication:

Vascular claudicationNeurogenic claudication
CauseInsufficient arterial supply to exercising muscleNeural compression
PatternReproducible exertional painOften affected by posture
ReliefStopping / rest — no change of position neededMay need sitting or spinal flexion
Advanced ischemia
CHRONIC LIMB-THREATENING ISCHEMIA (CLTI)
CLTI = advanced PAD with ischemic rest pain and/or tissue loss (ulcer or gangrene). Progression runs rest pain → ulceration → tissue loss → gangrene.

Assess: symptoms · walking / claudication distance · rest pain · tissue loss · overall disease severity.

  • Diabetic, leg pain and numbness after 500 m, must stop and rest to relieve it, normal neuro exam → vascular claudication. 438
Added explanationCalf claudication in a young non-smoker → think popliteal artery entrapment syndrome (the artery is compressed by the medial head of gastrocnemius) — atherosclerosis and Buerger's disease need risk factors (age, smoking).
Notes

Physical Examination

Examine the lower-limb pulses and look for evidence of chronic ischemia.

Notes

Ischemic / trophic changes

Dry skin
Loss of hair
Muscle wasting
Nail changes
Poor tissue quality
Ulceration, tissue loss, gangrene
Notes

Key signs

SignWhat you seeMechanism / meaning
Elevation pallorFoot turns pale when the leg is raisedInadequate arterial perfusion
Dependent ruborFoot turns red when loweredDilated ischemic vessels + increased dependent blood filling
UlcerTissue defect with a visible base; may be deep with exposed bone or necrosisTissue loss from chronic ischemia
GangreneTissue necrosisAdvanced ischemic damage
MEMORY HOOK
"Pale when up, red when down" — elevation pallor plus dependent rubor signals significant arterial insufficiency.
Added explanationIschaemic ulcers are on the toes/between the toes, heel and pressure points — painful, punched-out, pale base with poor granulation, cold pulseless foot. Venous ulcers are at the medial malleolus (gaiter area); neuropathic ulcers are painless, under the metatarsal heads.
Notes

Investigations

Three objectives:

1 · Diagnose & grade Confirm PAD and assess its severity.·2 · Systemic risk Lipids, glucose, BP etc. and associated systemic disease.·3 · Anatomy — if intervening Arterial anatomy and hemodynamic significance when intervention is considered.
Notes

Ankle–Brachial Index (ABI)

A simple, non-invasive, clinic-based test that gives objective evidence of PAD. ABI is a dimensionless ratio of ankle to brachial systolic pressure.

ABI =
Higher ankle systolic pressure (DP or PT) Higher brachial systolic pressure (either arm)

Measurement — six systolic readings:

2 BRACHIAL right + left arm·2 RIGHT ANKLE DP + PT·2 LEFT ANKLE DP + PT·= 6 READINGS → a right and a left ABI
PartRuleReason
DenominatorHigher brachial pressure, used for both legsReduces error from a unilateral upper-limb arterial stenosis
NumeratorHigher of DP / PT at each ankleOne numerator per leg
ResultSeparate right and left ABIsDon't simply divide right ankle by right arm
WORKED EXAMPLE
Brachial pressures 100 and 120 mmHg → denominator = 120 for both legs.
Ankle pressures 120 and 100 → ABI = 120 / 120 = 1.0 · Ankle pressures 50 and 60 → ABI = 60 / 120 = 0.5

Interpretation:

ABIMeaning
> 1.40Non-compressible (calcified) arteries — falsely high, not "excellent perfusion" (values of ~1.5, sometimes approaching 2)
1.00 – 1.40Normal
0.91 – 0.99Borderline
≤ 0.90PAD — the lower the ABI, the more severe the disease and the worse the cardiovascular risk
guideline values — check them against your lecture slides.Your notes were cut off at the start of this list (only the "~1.5, sometimes approaching 2" fragment survived), so these cut-offs are the standard guideline values — check them against your lecture slides.
PITFALL — THE FALSELY HIGH ABI
Calcified, non-compressible ankle arteries give a high ABI that does not reflect good perfusion. Use toe pressure / toe–brachial index (TBI) instead — digital arteries are less often heavily calcified. Lecture value: toe systolic ≥ 70 mmHg ≈ normal (toe pressure is normally lower than brachial).
  • How to calculate the ABI → ankle systolic BP / brachial systolic BP. 439
  • ABI 1.0 → normal. 439 ×2
Notes

Imaging modalities

Duplex US / colour DopplerCT angiographyMR angiographyCatheter angiography
ShowsStructure (US) + flow velocity & waveforms (Doppler) → anatomy and hemodynamicsDetailed, standardized anatomy; 3D reconstructionArterial anatomyStenosis / occlusion and distal flow
Radiation / contrastNeitherRadiation + IV contrast (needs IV access)No ionizing radiationInvasive arterial access
PracticalitiesInexpensive, painless, few consumablesRapid (~5 min); less operator-dependentExpensive, slow (often ≥ 30 min), motion- sensitiveProcedure-based
Main limitationOperator-dependent (probe position, angle, visualization)Contrast and radiation exposureLess practical in some patientsInvasive
Best useClarify uncertain findings; characterize diseasePlanning revascularization; extensive assessmentImaging without radiationWhen an endovascular procedure is planned
HOW DUPLEX WORKS
Ultrasound → vessel structure; Doppler → blood movement, from the frequency change of reflected waves.
The shift depends on flow direction, velocity and insonation angle.
A stenosis → ↑ local velocity and altered downstream waveforms.
WHEN TO IMAGE
Duplex — uncertain clinical findings; characterize the disease.
CTA / MRA — mainly when planning revascularization.
Catheter angiography — reserved for when endovascular treatment is planned.
Routine anatomic imaging is not needed for every stable PAD patient.
Notes

Relevant Arterial Anatomy

The arterial tree explains buttock vs thigh vs calf claudication and localizes the occlusive lesion. The external iliac becomes the common femoral beneath the inguinal ligament, then divides into the superficial femoral and profunda femoris.

Abdominal aorta

CLAUDICATION SITE

box colour = territory

Buttock / gluteal Aortoiliac / common iliac disease·Internal iliac pelvis · gluteal · perineal/penile·Common iliac·External iliac

inguinal ligament

Thigh External iliac / proximal femoral·Calf / leg More distal disease (SFA, popliteal, tibial)·Profunda femoris major thigh-muscle supply·Anterior tibial·Common femoral·Superficial femoral continues to distal limb·Popliteal·Posterior tibial·Peroneal (fibular)

Popliteal artery shown for continuity (standard anatomy; not listed in the lecture notes).

Added explanationLeriche syndrome (aortoiliac occlusion) = buttock/thigh claudication + absent femoral pulses + erectile dysfunction (impotence).
  • Most common cause of calf claudication in a 20-year-old non-smoker → popliteal entrapment syndrome. 427 ×2
Notes

PAD Management

Treatment goals

↓ MACE — heart & brain Major adverse cardiovascular events: MI, stroke, cardiovascular death.·↓ MALE — the limb Major adverse limb events: major amputation and serious limb events needing intervention.·For the patient Prolong survival · relieve ischemic symptoms · preserve the limb · improve quality of life.
RULE OF THUMB
Every PAD plan treats both the systemic cardiovascular risk and the local limb ischemia.
Notes

The treatment map

Smoking cessation Very important — smoking ↑ mortality & limb loss·Risk-factor control Aggressive control of diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia·Lifestyle Diet, weight control, regular exercise·PAD management·Antiplatelet therapy ↓ arterial thrombotic events·Statin For all PAD — even with normal cholesterol·Supervised exercise ≥ 3×/week walk–rest training·Revascularization Selected patients only — CLTI or refractory claudication
Added explanationBuerger's disease (thromboangiitis obliterans): young male heavy smokers, distal small/medium arteries (digital ischaemia, rest pain, ulcers, migratory superficial thrombophlebitis). Complete smoking cessation is the only treatment that halts it and prevents amputation.
Notes

Prevention & risk-factor modification

Primary prevention
Control risk factors to prevent atherosclerotic disease from developing.
Secondary prevention
Prevent progression and complications in established atherosclerosis — every PAD patient.
SMOKING CESSATION — VERY IMPORTANT
Continued smoking increases mortality and limb-loss risk; stopping improves outcomes. Adherence to medical therapy and lifestyle measures reduces both cardiovascular and limb complications.
  • What decreases mortality/progression in Buerger's disease → smoking cessation. 439
Notes

Antiplatelets & statins

ANTIPLATELET THERAPY
↓ platelet aggregation and arterial thrombosis at injured / atherosclerotic surfaces.
Goal: fewer cardiovascular and limb ischemic events — it does not remove established plaque.
STATINS — EVEN IF CHOLESTEROL IS NORMAL
↓ LDL and atherosclerotic risk; may also stabilize plaque and act anti-inflammatory.
The presence of atherosclerosis is the indication for intensive lipid-risk reduction — not a cholesterol above the normal range.
Notes

Supervised exercise therapy

≥ 3× PER WEEK·~30 min PER SESSION·3–4 min REST BETWEEN BOUTS

One session — repeated walk–rest cycles:

WALK Walk until claudication discomfort develops.→PUSH Continue into tolerable pain.→REST ~3–4 min, or until symptoms resolve.→REPEAT Resume walking; repeat for the whole session.
WHY IT WORKS
Aim: progressively increase pain-free and maximum walking distance. Benefits come from collateral circulation, muscle conditioning and better walking efficiency. Especially important in stable intermittent claudication — the goal is functional improvement, not muscle hypertrophy.

Regimen as given in the lecture.

Notes

Revascularization

Indications

REVASCULARIZE WHEN…
CLTI — rest pain, ulcers or tissue loss — and the limb is salvageable.
Lifestyle-limiting claudication persisting despite appropriate medical therapy and structured exercise.
AVOID EARLY INTERVENTION IN UNCOMPLICATED CLAUDICATION
Many patients improve with conservative management.
Endovascular repairs and bypass grafts have limited durability vs native vessels.
Ongoing smoking or uncontrolled risk factors worsen long-term results.
  • Bypass rather than conservative management → rest pain with gangrene of the toes (CLTI) — not claudication > 100 m, not a well-perfused or neuropathic ulcer. 439 ×6
  • Surgical rather than conservative → rest pain with gangrene of the toe (fragmentary recall). 427
  • Diabetic with a 1 × 2 cm forefoot ulcer and pain → keyed wound care and revascularization (both accepted); besides wound care, the most important step → revascularization. 439 ×5 439
Notes

Endovascular therapy: angioplasty ± stenting

1 Guidewire Passed through the stenotic / occluded segment.→2 Balloon angioplasty Inflation compresses / displaces plaque and expands the lumen.→RISK Recoil / re-narrowing The artery may recoil or re- narrow after dilation.→3 Stent Expandable mesh — radial force supports the wall and keeps the lumen patent.
Notes

Surgical bypass

Routes blood from a patent artery proximal to the obstruction to a suitable distal artery, bypassing the diseased segment.

Graft options: autologous vein or synthetic / prosthetic graft.
Autologous vein bypass often gives superior durability.
Suits long / complex lesions, unfavourable anatomy, or failed endovascular treatment.
More invasive — higher perioperative risk, more incisions, longer recovery.
Notes

Endovascular vs surgical bypass

Endovascular (angioplasty ± stent)Surgical bypass
Best suitedShort / focal lesionsLong / complex lesions; unfavourable anatomy; failed endovascular
InvasivenessLowerHigher — more incisions
Procedural riskLowerHigher perioperative risk
RecoveryFasterSlower
Long-term durabilityOften lower — restenosis / reocclusion, repeat interventionOften higher, especially with an autologous vein graft
Notes

Irreversible Ischemia & Amputation

Some patients present late, with extensive irreversible tissue necrosis — revascularization may no longer salvage the limb.

DANGER — REPERFUSING A DEAD LIMB
Restoring flow to severely necrotic / ischemic tissue washes accumulated toxins into the systemic circulation (reperfusion injury):
Washed out of necrotic tissueSystemic consequence
Potassium + acids / lactateHyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis → cardiac arrhythmias
MyoglobinAcute kidney injury
Toxic metabolitesARDS and systemic instability
Unsalvageable limb
→ Major amputation — commonly below-knee or above- knee, chosen by tissue viability and perfusion.
Limited tissue loss (e.g. one gangrenous toe)
→ Minor amputation / debridement + revascularization where appropriate — preserves the rest of the limb and lets the wound heal.
  • Sign supporting a non-healing ischaemic ulcer → between the 1st and 2nd toes, tender, with poor granulation tissue. 437 ×2
Notes

Mastery Checklist

1 PAD = marker of systemic atherosclerosis. These patients are more likely to have an MI or stroke (MI >
stroke) or die of cardiovascular causes than to need an amputation.
2 Most PAD is asymptomatic — limited activity can hide ischemia, so no claudication ≠ no significant disease.
3 Vascular claudication is reproducible exertional pain relieved by simply stopping; neurogenic is posture-
dependent and needs sitting or spinal flexion.
4 Site localizes the lesion: buttock → aortoiliac; thigh → external iliac / proximal femoral; calf → more distal
disease.
5 CLTI = ischemic rest pain and/or tissue loss (ulcer, gangrene) — the key indication to revascularize a
salvageable limb.
6 ABI = higher ankle pressure (DP or PT) ÷ higher brachial pressure (either arm), done for each leg. Low = worse
disease and CV risk; falsely high with calcified vessels → use toe pressure / TBI.
7 Duplex is cheap, painless, radiation- and contrast-free but operator-dependent; CTA / MRA mainly when
planning revascularization; catheter angiography when an endovascular procedure is planned.
8 Foundation for every patient: stop smoking, supervised exercise, statin (even with normal cholesterol),
antiplatelet, aggressive control of diabetes, BP and lipids.
9 Endovascular = less invasive, faster recovery, less durable (short / focal lesions); bypass = more durable,
especially autologous vein, but more invasive (long / complex lesions, failed endovascular).
10 Never reperfuse a dead limb: hyperkalemia, acidosis, arrhythmias, myoglobin-induced AKI and ARDS —
amputate instead (below- or above-knee by viability).
  • Calf claudication at 500 m, palpable femoral pulse, absent pulses below → next vascular test ankle–brachial index. 438 ×5
  • Calf claudication relieved by rest, ABI 0.60/0.65 → best medical therapy and supervised exercise first. 442 ×5
